Salesperson: Thanks for making time. We have about eight minutes. I'd like to understand your onboarding process, show where our workflow product might fit, and decide whether a small pilot is worth exploring. Does that match what you wanted from today?
Customer: Yes. We are a fictional logistics company, Northbridge Freight, with forty operations staff. We opened two depots this year. Training new coordinators is becoming harder, and I want a consistent process without giving everyone another system to maintain.
Salesperson: What happens today when a coordinator joins? Could you walk me through their first week, including who prepares their accounts and who checks that training is complete?
Customer: HR sends an email with a spreadsheet attached. The depot manager copies tasks into a local checklist. IT opens accounts when someone remembers to ask. We have a handbook, but its links are sometimes wrong. Nobody owns the whole process. A manager usually chases people on chat.
Salesperson: Where does that create the most trouble for your team?
Customer: Account access is the obvious one. Three of our last six starters waited more than two days for their scheduling account. They sat beside another coordinator instead of doing useful work. The manager loses time too. My bigger worry is a missed safety sign-off, although we have not had an incident.
Salesperson: That sounds frustrating. So you have delayed access and managers chasing tasks, plus a risk that safety checks get missed. Is there another issue you want us to account for?
Customer: Reporting. I cannot tell the operations director whether a person is ready without asking each depot. A shared view would help. But don't make managers spend ten minutes every day updating a dashboard. They will stop using it.
Salesperson: Our product has automated task reminders, templates, a dashboard, integrations, and an AI assistant. You can customize the interface with your logo, and we also have several permission levels and analytics charts.
Customer: Those features sound fine, but I need to understand what changes for a depot manager. We already bought a tool last year that looked impressive in a demo. The manager still had to enter the same information twice. We stopped using it after a month.
Salesperson: That's a useful warning. Let me make it concrete: a new-starter record can create assigned tasks from a depot template. The manager sees only blocked tasks instead of maintaining a separate spreadsheet. IT can acknowledge account completion in the same workflow. We would need to test your existing HR integration before promising that data entry disappears.
Customer: Good. We use a fairly old HR system, and I don't know if its API is included in our subscription. I can ask IT. If we have to copy employee records manually, I don't think this project will get approved.
Salesperson: Would a CSV import be enough as a temporary bridge while we investigate the API?
Customer: Maybe for a pilot, but not for the final rollout. I also have security concerns. These records include employee names and start dates. We need to know where the data is stored, who can access it, and whether your support staff can see it.
Salesperson: We can send a security document explaining hosting, access controls and support access. I don't want to give you an answer that I haven't checked. Could we include your IT security reviewer in a follow-up discussion?
Customer: Yes, I can invite our IT lead. They will want a retention policy too. We should probably avoid importing anything sensitive until they have reviewed your documentation.
Salesperson: Understood. For a pilot, we can use fictional employee records. What would make that pilot useful enough for you to recommend moving forward?
Customer: I'd want to see a manager create one starter, IT complete its tasks, and then get a readiness view without retyping the information. Faster access would be valuable. I haven't defined a numeric target yet. I would also need one depot manager to say that it is easier than the spreadsheet.
Salesperson: We can probably demonstrate that. Our starter plan is six hundred euros per month. Would that be within your budget?
Customer: I have not set a budget. The operations director would approve spending, and procurement may need to be involved. Six hundred might be reasonable if it saves enough manager time, but I cannot commit to it. I also need to understand whether implementation and support cost extra.
Salesperson: I'll send the pricing breakdown with any implementation costs identified. We can run the fictional-data pilot before discussing a contract.
Customer: That makes sense. We are trying to standardize onboarding before the next depot opens in September. I would prefer not to introduce a new process during the busiest summer weeks. We have some flexibility, but I need a realistic plan.
Salesperson: Let me summarize. You want reliable account setup, visible safety sign-offs, and a readiness view that does not create duplicate work. HR integration, security review and manager adoption need checking before this is useful. Is that a fair summary?
Customer: Yes, especially the duplicate entry. If the manager has to maintain two places, it won't last. I'd also like to compare your pilot workflow with what we can do in our existing HR tool. We haven't fully explored its onboarding module.
Salesperson: I'll email the security document and pricing breakdown by Thursday. You'll ask IT about the HR API and invite the IT lead. Could we tentatively meet next Tuesday afternoon to review those points and choose a pilot scenario?
Customer: Tuesday afternoon should work, but I need to check the IT lead's calendar before confirming. Send two time options. I can ask about the API before then. We are not agreeing to a pilot today, only to review whether one is worthwhile.
Salesperson: Agreed. I'll send two options with those documents, and we'll wait for your confirmation. Thanks for explaining the process so clearly.
